items.content_html:
To submit a Flink 2.2 SQL job in Application Mode on OpenShift without using the operator, you must leverage Flink’s Native Kubernetes Integration. Because traditional SQL command-line utilities require an active cluster session, you will build a custom Docker/Container image containing your Flink 2.2 dependencies, your SQL script, and a Java runner wrapper.

Apache.org OpenShift runs containers using arbitrary user IDs (Security Context Constraints), which requires proper file permissions in your image. Step 1: Download Flink 2.2 Compatible Connectors Flink 2.x enforces Java 17 and requires newer FLIP-27/FLIP-143 compliant connectors. Download the following .jar files and place them into a local directory named plugins/:

Apache Flink +1 Kafka Connector: flink-connector-kafka-.jar Kafka Clients: kafka-clients-.jar JDBC Connector: flink-connector-jdbc-.jar Database Driver: (e.g., postgresql-.jar or ojdbc*.jar)

Apache.org +1 Step 2: Build an OpenShift-Compliant Custom Image Create a Dockerfile that packages your Flink SQL configuration, connectors, and SQL file. Ensure files belong to root group 0 so OpenShift’s arbitrary user execution can read them. dockerfile FROM apache/flink:2.2.0-java17

Create standard Flink user directory structure

USER root RUN mkdir -p /opt/flink/usrlib /opt/flink/sql

Copy required connectors to the user library path

COPY plugins/*.jar /opt/flink/usrlib/

Copy your production SQL script

COPY pipeline.sql /opt/flink/sql/pipeline.sql

OpenShift compatibility: Grant group permissions to group 0

RUN chown -R flink:root /opt/flink/usrlib /opt/flink/sql &&
chmod -R g+rwX /opt/flink/usrlib /opt/flink/sql

USER 185 Use code with caution. Build and push this image to your OpenShift integrated registry or an external registry (like Quay or DockerHub): bash podman build -t quay.io/myorg/flink-sql-pipeline:2.2.0 . podman push quay.io/myorg/flink-sql-pipeline:2.2.0 Use code with caution. Step 3: Write Your Flink 2.2 SQL Pipeline (pipeline.sql) Define your Kafka source, JDBC lookup, and Kafka sink tables. Flink 2.2 supports high-performance Delta Joins and lookup cache tuning natively.

Apache.org +3 sql – 1. Kafka Source CREATE TABLE kafka_source ( user_id INT, item_id INT, behavior STRING, ts TIMESTAMP(3), proc_time AS PROCTIME() – Required for temporal lookup joins ) WITH ( ‘connector’ = ‘kafka’, ‘topic’ = ‘user_behaviors’, ‘properties.bootstrap.servers’ = ‘://apps-cluster.com’, ‘properties.group.id’ = ‘flink-sql-consumer’, ‘scan.startup.mode’ = ‘latest-offset’, ‘format’ = ‘json’ );

– 2. JDBC Reference Lookup Table CREATE TABLE jdbc_lookup ( item_id INT, item_name STRING, category STRING ) WITH ( ‘connector’ = ‘jdbc’, ‘url’ = ‘jdbc:postgresql://://apps-cluster.com’, ‘table-name’ = ‘items’, ‘username’ = ‘dbuser’, ‘password’ = ‘dbpassword’, ‘lookup.cache.max-rows’ = ‘5000’, ‘lookup.cache.ttl’ = ‘10min’ );

– 3. Kafka Sink CREATE TABLE kafka_sink ( user_id INT, item_name STRING, category STRING, behavior STRING ) WITH ( ‘connector’ = ‘kafka’, ‘topic’ = ‘enriched_behaviors’, ‘properties.bootstrap.servers’ = ‘://apps-cluster.com’, ‘format’ = ‘json’ );

– 4. Execution Logic (Enrichment Join) INSERT INTO kafka_sink SELECT s.user_id, l.item_name, l.category, s.behavior FROM kafka_source s LEFT JOIN jdbc_lookup FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF s.proc_time AS l ON s.item_id = l.item_id; Use code with caution. Step 4: Submit in Application Mode Using Flink Native CLI Since you are not using an operator, you must grant the default OpenShift ServiceAccount permissions to create Pods, Services, and ConfigMaps inside your project workspace so Flink’s JobManager can spin up TaskManagers. bash

Login to OpenShift and select your project namespace

oc login –token=XXXX –server=https://openshift.com oc project my-flink-jobs

Grant cluster permissions to your project’s default ServiceAccount

oc create rolebinding flink-pod-manager
–clusterrole=edit
–serviceaccount=my-flink-jobs:default
–namespace=my-flink-jobs Use code with caution. Now, unpack a standard Flink 2.2 distribution locally on your workstation to use its client CLI utility. Run the run-application command directly targeting the OpenShift Kubernetes API backend:

Apache.org bash ./bin/flink run-application
–target kubernetes-application
-Dkubernetes.cluster-id=flink-sql-kafka-jdbc-app
-Dkubernetes.container.image=quay.io/myorg/flink-sql-pipeline:2.2.0
-Dkubernetes.namespace=my-flink-jobs
-Dkubernetes.jobmanager.service-account=default
-Djobmanager.memory.process.size=2048m
-Dtaskmanager.memory.process.size=4096m
-Dtaskmanager.numberOfTaskSlots=2
-Dkubernetes.rest-service.exposed.type=ClusterIP
-c org.apache.flink.table.client.SqlClient
local:///opt/flink/opt/flink-sql-client-2.2.0.jar
-i /opt/flink/sql/pipeline.sql

Key Parameter Breakdowns: -target kubernetes-application: Signals Flink to bootstrap a dedicated single-job JobManager pod on OpenShift. -c org.apache.flink.table.client.SqlClient: Uses the embedded Flink SQL runner package already compiled inside the default Flink binary distribution framework. local://…: Prevents the client from uploading code; instead, forces the cluster to execute the .jar and .sql script natively packed inside your container image layer.

Apache.org

To secure your Flink 2.2 SQL pipeline, update your pipeline.sql configuration parameters to handle Kafka SASL authentication and connections to an Oracle database.

  1. Updated Kafka Tables with SASL Authentication Add Kafka configuration properties (properties.security.protocol, properties.sasl.mechanism, and properties.sasl.jaas.config) directly into your WITH clause. This example uses SASL_SSL and SCRAM-SHA-256, but you can change them to SASL_PLAINTEXT or PLAIN depending on your cluster setup. sql CREATE TABLE kafka_source ( user_id INT, item_id INT, behavior STRING, ts TIMESTAMP(3), proc_time AS PROCTIME() ) WITH ( ‘connector’ = ‘kafka’, ‘topic’ = ‘user_behaviors’, ‘properties.bootstrap.servers’ = ‘kafka-cluster-kafka-bootstrap:9092’, ‘properties.group.id’ = ‘flink-sql-consumer’, ‘scan.startup.mode’ = ‘latest-offset’, ‘format’ = ‘json’,

    – SASL Authentication Configurations ‘properties.security.protocol’ = ‘SASL_SSL’, ‘properties.sasl.mechanism’ = ‘SCRAM-SHA-256’, ‘properties.sasl.jaas.config’ = ‘org.apache.kafka.common.security.scram.ScramLoginModule required username=”my_kafka_user” password=”my_kafka_password”;’

); Use code with caution. (Apply the exact same three properties.security.* lines to your kafka_sink table definition as well). 2. Updated Oracle JDBC Reference Table Replace your PostgreSQL table configuration with the Oracle JDBC thin driver syntax. Ensure you map the exact uppercase or case-sensitive table schema names required by Oracle. sql CREATE TABLE jdbc_lookup ( item_id INT, item_name STRING, category STRING ) WITH ( ‘connector’ = ‘jdbc’, ‘url’ = ‘jdbc:oracle:thin:@//://apps-cluster.com’, ‘table-name’ = ‘MY_SCHEMA.ITEMS’, ‘username’ = ‘oracle_user’, ‘password’ = ‘oracle_password’, ‘lookup.cache.max-rows’ = ‘5000’, ‘lookup.cache.ttl’ = ‘10min’ ); Use code with caution. 3. Container Image Prerequisite Ensure you have downloaded the correct Oracle JDBC jar (e.g., ojdbc11.jar or ojdbc8.jar) and placed it inside your local plugins/ directory before building your Docker container image as described in the previous step. If you’d like to harden this setup, let me know: Do you want to inject these credentials securely via OpenShift Secrets and Flink dynamic parameters rather than hardcoding them in the SQL text? Do you need to append TrustStore / KeyStore certificates (properties.ssl.truststore.location) for Kafka’s SSL handshake?

yes to both your questions To secure your production Flink 2.2 deployment on OpenShift without hardcoding credentials, you can leverage OpenShift Secrets mapped as environment variables and files inside your pods. Flink 2.2 natively allows referencing environment variables directly inside the SQL script using string interpolation syntax like ${env:VAR_NAME}. The architecture uses an OpenShift Secret to hold the sensitive Kafka credentials, the Kafka SSL TrustStore file, and the Oracle DB username/password. Step 1: Create the OpenShift Secret Prepare your Kafka SSL TrustStore file locally (kafka.truststore.jks). Then, create a single OpenShift secret containing your passwords, usernames, and the binary truststore file: bash oc create secret generic flink-stream-secrets
–from-literal=kafka-user=’my_kafka_user’
–from-literal=kafka-password=’my_kafka_password’
–from-literal=oracle-user=’oracle_user’
–from-literal=oracle-password=’oracle_password’
–from-file=kafka.truststore.jks=./kafka.truststore.jks
–namespace=my-flink-jobs Use code with caution. Step 2: Parametrize pipeline.sql using Environment Variables Update your SQL code to completely remove plaintext strings. Flink 2.2 will parse ${env:VARIABLE_NAME} at runtime before executing the graph. sql – 1. Kafka Source with SASL_SSL and TrustStore CREATE TABLE kafka_source ( user_id INT, item_id INT, behavior STRING, ts TIMESTAMP(3), proc_time AS PROCTIME() ) WITH ( ‘connector’ = ‘kafka’, ‘topic’ = ‘user_behaviors’, ‘properties.bootstrap.servers’ = ‘kafka-cluster-kafka-bootstrap:9092’, ‘properties.group.id’ = ‘flink-sql-consumer’, ‘scan.startup.mode’ = ‘latest-offset’, ‘format’ = ‘json’,

-- SASL Configuration using Environment Variables
'properties.security.protocol' = 'SASL_SSL',
'properties.sasl.mechanism' = 'SCRAM-SHA-256',
'properties.sasl.jaas.config' = 'org.apache.kafka.common.security.scram.ScramLoginModule required username="${env:KAFKA_USER}" password="${env:KAFKA_PASS}";',

-- SSL TrustStore Configurations using Mounted Secret Path
'properties.ssl.truststore.location' = '/opt/flink/secrets/kafka.truststore.jks',
'properties.ssl.truststore.password' = '${env:KAFKA_PASS}' -- Or separate var if passwords differ

);

– 2. Oracle Lookup Table CREATE TABLE jdbc_lookup ( item_id INT, item_name STRING, category STRING ) WITH ( ‘connector’ = ‘jdbc’, ‘url’ = ‘jdbc:oracle:thin:@//://apps-cluster.com’, ‘table-name’ = ‘MY_SCHEMA.ITEMS’, ‘username’ = ‘${env:ORACLE_USER}’, ‘password’ = ‘${env:ORACLE_PASS}’, ‘lookup.cache.max-rows’ = ‘5000’, ‘lookup.cache.ttl’ = ‘10min’ );

– 3. Kafka Sink CREATE TABLE kafka_sink ( user_id INT, item_name STRING, category STRING, behavior STRING ) WITH ( ‘connector’ = ‘kafka’, ‘topic’ = ‘enriched_behaviors’, ‘properties.bootstrap.servers’ = ‘kafka-cluster-kafka-bootstrap:9092’, ‘format’ = ‘json’, ‘properties.security.protocol’ = ‘SASL_SSL’, ‘properties.sasl.mechanism’ = ‘SCRAM-SHA-256’, ‘properties.sasl.jaas.config’ = ‘org.apache.kafka.common.security.scram.ScramLoginModule required username=”${env:KAFKA_USER}” password=”${env:KAFKA_PASS}”;’, ‘properties.ssl.truststore.location’ = ‘/opt/flink/secrets/kafka.truststore.jks’, ‘properties.ssl.truststore.password’ = ‘${env:KAFKA_PASS}’ );

– Execution INSERT INTO kafka_sink SELECT s.user_id, l.item_name, l.category, s.behavior FROM kafka_source s LEFT JOIN jdbc_lookup FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF s.proc_time AS l ON s.item_id = l.item_id; Use code with caution. Step 3: Inject Secrets into the Native Flink CLI Submission When executing flink run-application, pass specific -D flags that instruct the Native Flink Kubernetes coordinator to inject env variables and volume mounts into both the JobManager and TaskManager pods. bash ./bin/flink run-application
–target kubernetes-application
-Dkubernetes.cluster-id=flink-secure-pipeline
-Dkubernetes.container.image=quay.io/myorg/flink-sql-pipeline:2.2.0
-Dkubernetes.namespace=my-flink-jobs
-Dkubernetes.jobmanager.service-account=default
-Djobmanager.memory.process.size=2048m
-Dtaskmanager.memory.process.size=4096m
-Dtaskmanager.numberOfTaskSlots=2

– 1. Map Secret keys as Environment Variables to JobManager Pod -Dkubernetes.jobmanager.env.KAFKA_USER=fromSecret:flink-stream-secrets:kafka-user
-Dkubernetes.jobmanager.env.KAFKA_PASS=fromSecret:flink-stream-secrets:kafka-password
-Dkubernetes.jobmanager.env.ORACLE_USER=fromSecret:flink-stream-secrets:oracle-user
-Dkubernetes.jobmanager.env.ORACLE_PASS=fromSecret:flink-stream-secrets:oracle-password

– 2. Map Secret keys as Environment Variables to TaskManager Pods -Dkubernetes.taskmanager.env.KAFKA_USER=fromSecret:flink-stream-secrets:kafka-user
-Dkubernetes.taskmanager.env.KAFKA_PASS=fromSecret:flink-stream-secrets:kafka-password
-Dkubernetes.taskmanager.env.ORACLE_USER=fromSecret:flink-stream-secrets:oracle-user
-Dkubernetes.taskmanager.env.ORACLE_PASS=fromSecret:flink-stream-secrets:oracle-password

– 3. Mount Secret as a File Volume (For the TrustStore .jks binary) -Dkubernetes.secrets=flink-stream-secrets:/opt/flink/secrets

-c org.apache.flink.table.client.SqlClient
local:///opt/flink/opt/flink-sql-client-2.2.0.jar
-i /opt/flink/sql/pipeline.sql Use code with caution. Verification Checklist File Permissions: The volume mounted at /opt/flink/secrets will implicitly carry read access for group 0, aligning with OpenShift’s arbitrary UID runtime constraints. Dynamic Evaluation: Flink evaluates ${env:…} variables inside the JobManager task compiler context immediately before launching execution topologies, keeping variables completely omitted from logs and checkpoint metadata. show mr how to use the connectors with java pipeline To transition your Flink 2.2 pipeline from SQL to a programmatic Java DataStream Application, you will utilize the newer FLIP-27 KafkaSource, FLIP-143 KafkaSink, and the updated Flink 2.x JDBC compilation API. The configuration pattern below mirrors the OpenShift environment variable injection and TrustStore setup we built previously. Step 1: Update your Maven pom.xml Dependencies Flink 2.2 requires Java 17 and distinct connector dependencies. Make sure your pom.xml includes these artifacts: xml org.apache.flink flink-streaming-java 2.2.0 provided 

<!-- Flink Kafka Connector -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.flink</groupId>
    <artifactId>flink-connector-kafka</artifactId>
    <version>3.4.0-2.2</version> <!-- Match the Flink 2.2 compatible connector version -->
</dependency>

<!-- Flink JDBC Connector -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.flink</groupId>
    <artifactId>flink-connector-jdbc</artifactId>
    <version>3.2.0-2.2</version> <!-- Match the Flink 2.2 compatible connector version -->
</dependency>

<!-- Oracle JDBC Driver -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.oracle.database.jdbc</groupId>
    <artifactId>ojdbc11</artifactId>
    <version>23.3.0.23.09</version>
</dependency>
Use code with caution. Step 2: Implement the Java Pipeline Application This Java implementation reads your injected OpenShift environment variables, configures the Kafka source with SASL/SSL, invokes an asynchronous lookup or traditional map join against Oracle, and writes out to the secured Kafka sink. java package com.myorg.flink;

import org.apache.flink.api.common.eventtime.WatermarkStrategy; import org.apache.flink.api.common.serialization.SimpleStringSchema; import org.apache.flink.connector.kafka.sink.KafkaRecordSerializationSchema; import org.apache.flink.connector.kafka.sink.KafkaSink; import org.apache.flink.connector.kafka.source.KafkaSource; import org.apache.flink.connector.kafka.source.enumerator.initializer.OffsetsInitializer; import org.apache.flink.connector.jdbc.JdbcConnectionOptions; import org.apache.flink.streaming.api.datastream.DataStream; import org.apache.flink.streaming.api.environment.StreamExecutionEnvironment; import java.util.Properties;

public class SecureFlinkPipeline {

public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    // 1. Initialize Flink Execution Environment
    final StreamExecutionEnvironment env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment();

    // 2. Fetch OpenShift Injected Environment Variables
    String kafkaUser = System.getenv("KAFKA_USER");
    String kafkaPass = System.getenv("KAFKA_PASS");
    String oracleUser = System.getenv("ORACLE_USER");
    String oraclePass = System.getenv("ORACLE_PASS");
    
    // Path to the mounted OpenShift Secret Volume
    String truststoreLocation = "/opt/flink/secrets/kafka.truststore.jks";

    // 3. Construct JAAS and SSL Security Properties for Kafka
    Properties kafkaProps = new Properties();
    kafkaProps.setProperty("security.protocol", "SASL_SSL");
    kafkaProps.setProperty("sasl.mechanism", "SCRAM-SHA-256");
    kafkaProps.setProperty("sasl.jaas.config", 
        "org.apache.kafka.common.security.scram.ScramLoginModule required username=\"" 
        + kafkaUser + "\" password=\"" + kafkaPass + "\";");
    kafkaProps.setProperty("ssl.truststore.location", truststoreLocation);
    kafkaProps.setProperty("ssl.truststore.password", kafkaPass);

    // 4. Configure Secure Kafka Source (FLIP-27 API)
    KafkaSource<String> kafkaSource = KafkaSource.<String>builder()
            .setBootstrapServers("kafka-cluster-kafka-bootstrap:9092")
            .setTopics("user_behaviors")
            .setGroupId("flink-java-consumer")
            .setStartingOffsets(OffsetsInitializer.latest())
            .setValueOnlyDeserializer(new SimpleStringSchema())
            .setProperties(kafkaProps)
            .build();

    // Create the Input DataStream
    DataStream<String> kafkaStream = env.fromSource(
            kafkaSource, 
            WatermarkStrategy.noWatermarks(), 
            "Kafka Secure Source"
    );

    // 5. Oracle JDBC Connection Configuration (FLIP-143 Ready Pattern)
    JdbcConnectionOptions jdbcOptions = new JdbcConnectionOptions.JdbcConnectionOptionsBuilder()
            .withUrl("jdbc:oracle:thin:@//://apps-cluster.com")
            .withDriverName("oracle.jdbc.OracleDriver")
            .withUsername(oracleUser)
            .withPassword(oraclePass)
            .build();

    // 6. Enrich Stream via a Custom Mapping or RichFunction
    // (Note: For low-latency temporal lookups, implement a RichAsyncFunction querying Oracle using jdbcOptions)
    DataStream<String> enrichedStream = kafkaStream.map(new OracleEnrichmentMapFunction(jdbcOptions));

    // 7. Configure Secure Kafka Sink (FLIP-143 API)
    KafkaSink<String> kafkaSink = KafkaSink.<String>builder()
            .setBootstrapServers("kafka-cluster-kafka-bootstrap:9092")
            .setRecordSerializer(
                    KafkaRecordSerializationSchema.builder()
                            .setTopic("enriched_behaviors")
                            .setValueSerializationSchema(new SimpleStringSchema())
                            .build()
            )
            .setKafkaProducerConfig(kafkaProps) // Reuses the secure JAAS/SSL properties
            .build();

    // Direct stream to the Secure Sink
    enrichedStream.sinkTo(kafkaSink);

    // Execute the Application Pipeline
    env.execute("Secure-Flink-2.2-Java-Pipeline");
}

} Use code with caution. Step 3: Modify your Image Build (Dockerfile) Since your dependencies and logic are now compiled into a single heavy application artifact, change your Dockerfile to copy your compiled .jar instead of loose plugin dependencies. dockerfile FROM apache/flink:2.2.0-java17

chmod -R g+rwX /opt/flink/usrlib /opt/flink/secrets

If you need more help with the code implementation, tell me: Would you like an example of the OracleEnrichmentMapFunction code, or are you looking to use Flink Async I/O to prevent blocking pipeline execution during database lookups? Do you need to parse the Kafka source message into a specific object schema like Avro/Schema Registry or standard JSON POJO objects?

yes to both question Here is the implementation of the OracleEnrichmentMapFunction using Flink Async I/O (which avoids blocking your streaming threads during database queries) along with standard JSON POJO parsing for incoming Kafka events. Step 1: Add Jackson Dependency for JSON Parsing To parse your JSON messages into Java POJOs, add the Jackson library to your Maven pom.xml if it isn’t already included by your Flink dependencies: xml com.fasterxml.jackson.core jackson-databind 2.17.2 Use code with caution. Step 2: Define your POJO Models Create standard Java objects representing your incoming raw data and your final enriched output. java package com.myorg.flink.model;

import java.io.Serializable;

// 1. Raw Event Model from Kafka Source public class UserBehavior implements Serializable { public int user_id; public int item_id; public String behavior; public String ts;

public UserBehavior() {} // Required default constructor for Jackson/Flink POJO serialization

} Use code with caution. java package com.myorg.flink.model;

import java.io.Serializable;

// 2. Enriched Event Model for Kafka Sink public class EnrichedBehavior implements Serializable { public int user_id; public String item_name; public String category; public String behavior;

public EnrichedBehavior() {}

public EnrichedBehavior(int user_id, String item_name, String category, String behavior) {
    this.user_id = user_id;
    this.item_name = item_name;
    this.category = category;
    this.behavior = behavior;
}

} Use code with caution. Step 3: Implement Async I/O for Oracle DB Lookup Using RichAsyncFunction allows Flink to concurrent-fire lookups to Oracle using an internal thread pool. This prevents a slow DB query from causing backpressure across your entire pipeline. java package com.myorg.flink.functions;

import com.myorg.flink.model.EnrichedBehavior; import com.myorg.flink.model.UserBehavior; import org.apache.flink.configuration.Configuration; import org.apache.flink.connector.jdbc.JdbcConnectionOptions; import org.apache.flink.streaming.api.functions.async.ResultFuture; import org.apache.flink.streaming.api.functions.async.RichAsyncFunction;

import java.sql.Connection; import java.sql.DriverManager; import java.sql.PreparedStatement; import java.sql.ResultSet; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public class OracleAsyncLookupFunction extends RichAsyncFunction<UserBehavior, EnrichedBehavior> {

private final JdbcConnectionOptions jdbcOptions;
private transient Connection connection;
private transient PreparedStatement preparedStatement;
private transient ExecutorService executorService;

public OracleAsyncLookupFunction(JdbcConnectionOptions jdbcOptions) {
    this.jdbcOptions = jdbcOptions;
}

@Override
public void open(Configuration parameters) throws Exception {
    super.open(parameters);
    // Load Driver and establish the base connection
    Class.forName(jdbcOptions.getDriverName());
    this.connection = DriverManager.getConnection(
            jdbcOptions.getDbURL(), 
            jdbcOptions.getUsername().orElse(null), 
            jdbcOptions.getPassword().orElse(null)
    );
    
    // Prepare your SQL compilation ahead of time
    String query = "SELECT item_name, category FROM MY_SCHEMA.ITEMS WHERE item_id = ?";
    this.preparedStatement = connection.prepareStatement(query);
    
    // Thread pool to handle non-blocking asynchronous execution loops
    this.executorService = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);
}

@Override
public void asyncInvoke(UserBehavior input, ResultFuture<EnrichedBehavior> resultFuture) {
    // Issue queries to the thread pool to avoid blocking Flink's stream thread
    executorService.submit(() -> {
        try {
            // Synchronize the prepared statement use since it's shared across the pool
            ResultSet resultSet;
            synchronized (preparedStatement) {
                preparedStatement.setInt(1, input.item_id);
                resultSet = preparedStatement.executeQuery();
            }

            String itemName = "UNKNOWN";
            String category = "UNKNOWN";

            if (resultSet.next()) {
                itemName = resultSet.getString("item_name");
                category = resultSet.getString("category");
            }
            resultSet.close();

            // Construct enriched object and emit
            EnrichedBehavior output = new EnrichedBehavior(
                    input.user_id, 
                    itemName, 
                    category, 
                    input.behavior
            );
            
            resultFuture.complete(Collections.singletonList(output));
            
        } catch (Exception e) {
            // Handle or pass failures gracefully to avoid crushing your container topology
            resultFuture.completeExceptionally(e);
        }
    });
}

@Override
public void close() throws Exception {
    if (preparedStatement != null) preparedStatement.close();
    if (connection != null) connection.close();
    if (executorService != null) executorService.shutdown();
    super.close();
}
